evaporation-001.question: When a solution is concentrated in an evaporator, which statement about the steam used for heating (live steam) and the vapor generated from the solution is correct?
choices: The live steam condenses across the heat transfer surface, giving its latent heat to the solution, and the generated vapor is condensed or used to heat the next body
The live steam is blown directly into the solution and concentrated together with it, so its condensate ends up as part of the concentrated product
The generated vapor has the same temperature and pressure as the live steam, so it can be returned directly to heat the same evaporator without any compression at all
evaporation-001.explanation: In an evaporator, the heating steam (live steam) condenses in the steam chest across the heat transfer surface, and its latent heat boils the solution. The condensate is discharged separately from the solution, so the product is not diluted. The vapor generated from the solution (secondary vapor) is solvent vapor; it is condensed in a condenser and discarded, or used as heating steam for the next body at lower pressure. This is the idea of multiple-effect evaporation. Blowing live steam directly into the solution would dilute it with condensate, which defeats the purpose of concentrating. The generated vapor is lower in both temperature and pressure than the live steam by the temperature difference needed for heat transfer, so it cannot heat the same body as it is; it must be compressed to raise its condensing temperature (MVR or thermal vapor recompression).

evaporation-002.question: An aqueous solution containing a nonvolatile solute is concentrated in an evaporator. How does a large boiling-point elevation of the solution affect heat transfer (the live steam temperature and evaporator pressure are unchanged)?
choices: The condensing temperature of the generated vapor rises by the boiling-point elevation, so the effective temperature difference becomes larger
The boiling point of the solution is fixed by the evaporator pressure alone, so the effective temperature difference does not change
The solution boils at a higher temperature than water at the same pressure, so the effective temperature difference to the live steam is smaller by the boiling-point elevation
evaporation-002.explanation: A nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent, so at the same pressure the solution does not boil until it is hotter than pure water. This is boiling-point elevation. The driving force for heat transfer is the difference between the condensing temperature of the live steam and the boiling point of the solution, so the effective temperature difference is reduced by the boiling-point elevation, and a larger heat transfer area is needed to transfer the same heat. A boiling point fixed by pressure alone applies to a pure solvent; for a solution it also changes with concentration. The generated vapor leaves at the boiling point of the solution, but because it is pure solvent vapor it condenses at the saturation temperature of water at the evaporator pressure. The vapor is merely superheated by the boiling-point elevation; its condensing temperature is not raised. For concentrated sodium hydroxide solutions and the like, the boiling-point elevation reaches several tens of K.

evaporation-003.question: In a single-effect evaporator, the heating steam condenses at 120 ℃. The saturation temperature of water at the evaporator pressure is 60 ℃, and the boiling-point elevation of the concentrate is 8 K. What is the effective temperature difference available for heat transfer?
evaporation-003.explanation: The solution boils at 60 + 8 = 68 ℃, higher than the saturation temperature of water by the boiling-point elevation, so the effective temperature difference is 120 − 68 = 52 K. 60 K is the difference between the heating steam and the saturation temperature of water, 120 − 60, ignoring the boiling-point elevation. Using this apparent temperature difference underestimates the heat transfer area and gives an evaporator that falls short of capacity. 68 K adds the boiling-point elevation where it should be subtracted (120 − 60 + 8). Note also that deep below the liquid surface the hydrostatic head of the liquid raises the boiling point further, so in a tall body the effective temperature difference can be smaller than this.

evaporation-004.question: The boiling point of an aqueous salt solution (at fixed concentration) is 70 ℃ at the pressure where water boils at 50 ℃, and 125 ℃ at the pressure where water boils at 100 ℃. Using Dühring's rule (the boiling point of a solution of given concentration is linear in the boiling point of water at the same pressure), what is the approximate boiling point of the solution at the pressure where water boils at 80 ℃?
choices: About 103 ℃
About 100 ℃
About 105 ℃
evaporation-004.explanation: A Dühring line is a straight line with the boiling point of water on the horizontal axis and that of the solution on the vertical axis. It passes through (50, 70) and (100, 125), so its slope is (125 − 70)/(100 − 50) = 1.1, and at a water boiling point of 80 ℃ the solution boils at 70 + 1.1 × (80 − 50) = 103 ℃. The boiling-point elevation is 20 K at a water boiling point of 50 ℃, 23 K at 80 ℃ and 25 K at 100 ℃, increasing with pressure. About 100 ℃ assumes the low-pressure elevation of 20 K applies at every pressure, and about 105 ℃ uses the high-pressure value of 25 K. For solutions whose Dühring line has a slope other than 1, treating the boiling-point elevation as constant introduces error.

evaporation-005.question: A 10 wt% aqueous solution is fed to an evaporator at 6000 kg/h and concentrated to 40 wt% (nonvolatile solute, steady state). How much water must be evaporated?
evaporation-005.explanation: The solute does not evaporate, so 6000 × 0.10 = 600 kg/h of solute stays in the concentrate. The concentrate amounts to 600/0.40 = 1500 kg/h, so the evaporation is 6000 − 1500 = 4500 kg/h. As a formula, evaporation = F(1 − x_F/x_P) = 6000 × (1 − 0.25). 1500 kg/h is the amount of concentrate (product), mistaken for the evaporation. 1800 kg/h multiplies the feed by the concentration difference 0.40 − 0.10, confusing a difference in concentration with a fraction of the flow. In evaporator calculations the basic approach is first to fix the amount of concentrate from the solute balance and then to find the steam from the energy balance.

evaporation-006.question: When the same evaporator evaporates the same amount of water, which statement correctly compares feeding the solution well below its boiling point with feeding it at its boiling point (neglect heat losses)?
choices: The cold feed condenses part of the generated vapor and recovers its heat, so the steam economy actually improves
Extra live steam is needed for the sensible heat to bring the feed to its boiling point, so the steam economy (evaporation per kg of live steam) falls
The live steam required is fixed only by the latent heat of the water evaporated, so it does not depend on the feed temperature
evaporation-006.explanation: In the energy balance of an evaporator, the heat released by the condensing live steam covers the sensible heat to bring the feed to its boiling point plus the latent heat to evaporate the water. A cold feed needs more live steam for the sensible heat, so the steam economy falls for the same evaporation. Treating the steam requirement as fixed by the latent heat alone applies only to the special case of a feed entering at its boiling point. The heat that warms the cold feed ultimately comes from the live steam as well, so the steam economy cannot improve. Conversely, when a feed above its boiling point enters a lower-pressure body, part of it flashes and evaporates, which raises the steam economy. Preheating the feed with the heat of the condensate or the concentrate is therefore a basic energy-saving measure.

evaporation-007.question: A feed of 10000 kg/h at 20 ℃ (specific heat 3.9 kJ/(kg·K)) enters a single-effect evaporator, and 6000 kg/h of water is evaporated at a boiling point of 70 ℃. Take the latent heat of evaporation of water at 70 ℃ as 2330 kJ/kg and the condensing latent heat of the heating steam as 2200 kJ/kg, and neglect boiling-point elevation, heat of concentration and heat losses. Approximately how much heating steam is needed?
choices: About 7240 kg/h
About 6350 kg/h
About 6000 kg/h
evaporation-007.explanation: The heat needed is the sensible heat to warm the feed from 20 ℃ to 70 ℃, 10000 × 3.9 × 50 = 1.95×10⁶ kJ/h, plus the latent heat to evaporate 6000 kg/h of water, 6000 × 2330 = 1.398×10⁷ kJ/h, giving 1.593×10⁷ kJ/h. Dividing by the condensing latent heat of 2200 kJ/kg gives about 7240 kg/h of heating steam and a steam economy of 6000/7240 ≈ 0.83. About 6350 kg/h forgets the sensible heat of the feed and uses the latent heat alone (6000 × 2330/2200). About 6000 kg/h assumes that 1 kg of steam evaporates 1 kg of water, leaving out both the difference in latent heats and the sensible heat. In a single effect the steam economy is normally below 1.

evaporation-008.question: N evaporator bodies, each with the same heat transfer area as a single-effect unit, are arranged as a multiple-effect evaporator (the live steam temperature and the condensing temperature of the last effect are the same as for the single effect, and the overall heat transfer coefficients are similar). Which statement correctly describes it compared with the single effect?
choices: Both the steam economy and the evaporating capacity (evaporation per hour) increase roughly in proportion to the number of effects N
The overall temperature difference is unchanged, so the steam economy is almost the same as for a single effect
The steam economy rises roughly in proportion to N, but the N bodies share the overall temperature difference, so the total evaporating capacity is not much different from that of a single effect
evaporation-008.explanation: In a multiple-effect evaporator the vapor from one body heats the next, so 1 kg of live steam evaporates close to N kg of water and the steam economy rises roughly in proportion to N (somewhat less than N in practice because of boiling-point elevation and sensible heat). On the other hand, the effective temperature difference of each body is the overall temperature difference, from the live steam to the condensing temperature of the last effect, divided among the N bodies. Each body transfers about U·A·ΔT/N, so the total for the N bodies is about the same as U·A·ΔT for the single effect, and the capacity does not increase. Multiple-effect evaporation is a way of reducing steam (operating cost) by adding heat transfer area (equipment cost). Saying that the capacity also grows with N overlooks how the temperature difference is shared, and saying that the steam economy is unchanged overlooks the reuse of the vapor.

evaporation-009.question: In a triple-effect evaporator, the sum of the effective temperature differences, after subtracting boiling-point elevations, is 55 K. Assume the effects have equal heat transfer areas and transfer equal amounts of heat. If the overall heat transfer coefficients are 3000, 2000 and 1200 W/(m²·K) in the first, second and third effects, what is the approximate effective temperature difference in the third effect?
choices: About 10.6 K
About 27.5 K
About 18.3 K
evaporation-009.explanation: Since Q = U·A·ΔT is the same in every effect and A is also the same, ΔT is inversely proportional to U. The ratio of 1/U is 1/3000 : 1/2000 : 1/1200 = 2 : 3 : 5, so dividing 55 K in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5 gives 11 K in the first effect, 16.5 K in the second and 27.5 K in the third. The last effect handles the most concentrated liquid at the lowest temperature, so its viscosity is high and U tends to be small, which calls for a large temperature difference. About 10.6 K divides ΔT in proportion to U (55 × 1200/6200), which reverses the relation. Because U is smallest in the third effect, making ΔT proportional to U wrongly gives it the smallest temperature difference. About 18.3 K splits 55 K into three equal parts, ignoring the differences in U.

evaporation-010.question: In a multiple-effect evaporator handling a solution whose viscosity rises sharply as it is concentrated, what is the main reason backward feed (feed enters the last effect and product is withdrawn from the first effect) is better than forward feed?
choices: The most concentrated, viscous liquid is handled in the hottest first effect, lowering its viscosity and limiting the drop in heat transfer coefficient
The liquid flows between effects by the pressure difference alone, so no pumps are needed even to move it from the low-pressure side to the high-pressure side
A heat-sensitive product can be finished in the coolest last effect, which limits thermal degradation of the product
evaporation-010.explanation: Viscosity increases with concentration and decreases with temperature. In backward feed, the most concentrated liquid is in the hot first effect heated by live steam, so the rise in viscosity is offset and the heat transfer coefficient is easier to maintain. Because the cold feed enters the cool last effect, there is also the advantage that high-temperature heat is not spent warming the feed. However, the liquid must be moved from the low-pressure side to the high-pressure side, so pumps are needed between effects. Flow by pressure difference alone without pumps is a feature of forward feed, which sends the liquid from the high-pressure first effect to the lower-pressure effects. Finishing a heat-sensitive product at low temperature is also an advantage of forward feed; in backward feed the product is exposed to the highest temperature.

evaporation-011.question: A double-effect evaporator (forward feed) receives 10000 kg/h of a 5 wt% aqueous solution at the boiling point of the first effect and concentrates it to 20 wt%. Take the latent heat of evaporation as 2300 kJ/kg in both effects, the specific heat of the liquid as 4.0 kJ/(kg·K) and the difference between the boiling points of the first and second effects as 30 K, and neglect boiling-point elevation and heat losses. Approximately how much live steam is needed?
choices: About 3750 kg/h
About 3920 kg/h
About 3580 kg/h
evaporation-011.explanation: The total evaporation is 10000 × (1 − 5/20) = 7500 kg/h. The feed enters at its boiling point and the latent heats are equal everywhere, so the live steam S equals the evaporation in the first effect, V₁. The liquid leaving the first effect, 10000 − V₁, partly flashes when it enters the second effect, which is 30 K cooler, so the energy balance of the second effect is V₁ × 2300 + (10000 − V₁) × 4.0 × 30 = V₂ × 2300. Solving this with V₁ + V₂ = 7500 gives the live steam S = V₁ ≈ 3580 kg/h (steam economy about 2.09). About 3750 kg/h ignores the flash and splits 7500 in two, and about 3920 kg/h is the evaporation in the second effect, V₂ = 7500 − 3580, mistaken for the live steam.

evaporation-012.question: Which statement about a mechanical vapor recompression (MVR) evaporator is correct?
choices: All of the generated vapor is drawn into a steam ejector driven by high-pressure live steam and returned to heat the same body without producing any surplus vapor at all
The generated vapor is compressed, e.g. electrically, to raise its condensing temperature and returned to heat the same body, so little live steam is needed in steady operation
The larger the boiling-point elevation, the smaller the compression ratio needed because the generated vapor is already superheated, so such solutions are favorable
evaporation-012.explanation: MVR raises the pressure of the generated vapor with a compressor so that its saturation temperature is above the boiling point of the solution, and condenses it in the steam chest of the same body. Because the latent heat of evaporation is reused over and over, the main external input is the compressor power, and live steam is used only a little, at start-up or to make up heat losses. The saturation temperature must be raised by the effective temperature difference plus the boiling-point elevation, so the larger the boiling-point elevation, the higher the compression ratio and the power, which is a disadvantage. MVR is therefore suited to concentrating solutions with a small boiling-point elevation at a small temperature difference. Drawing in the generated vapor with a steam ejector is thermal vapor recompression (TVR), which is driven by high-pressure live steam.

evaporation-013.question: Which statement about a thermal vapor recompression (TVR) evaporator using a steam ejector (thermocompressor) is correct?
choices: All of the generated vapor is drawn in and returned for heating, so no surplus vapor goes to a condenser or the next effect and the steam economy approaches infinity as a result
The generated vapor is compressed by an electric compressor, so apart from start-up no live steam is used and no surplus vapor arises
High-pressure live steam serves as the motive flow to draw in part of the generated vapor, and the mixture does the heating, raising the steam economy for the same number of effects
evaporation-013.explanation: In TVR, high-pressure live steam is jetted from the ejector nozzle, its momentum draws in part of the generated vapor, and the mixture of the two is used for heating. The latent heat of the vapor drawn in is reused, so if, for example, 1 kg of motive steam draws in 1 kg of generated vapor, even a single effect ideally reaches a steam economy of about 2. It has no moving parts and is inexpensive, but because it is driven by live steam, surplus vapor roughly equal to the motive steam added is always produced and must be sent to a condenser or the next effect. This is why not all of the generated vapor can be returned. Compression by an electric compressor is mechanical vapor recompression (MVR); TVR compresses only with the energy of the live steam.

evaporation-014.question: Which evaporator type is best suited to concentrating heat-sensitive fruit juices or dairy products with a short residence time?
choices: The falling-film type, in which the liquid flows down the inner wall of the heating tubes as a thin film
The short-tube vertical (standard) type, in which the liquid circulates naturally through the heating tubes and a large amount of liquid is held in the body
The forced-circulation type, in which a pump circulates the liquid at a high flow rate and boiling is suppressed inside the tubes
evaporation-014.explanation: In a falling-film evaporator, the liquid is fed to the top of the heating tubes and flows down the inner wall as a thin film, evaporating in a single pass. The liquid holdup is small and the residence time short, and there is almost no rise in boiling point from hydrostatic head, so it can be operated at a small temperature difference and low temperature, which suits heat-sensitive liquids. The short-tube vertical type holds a large amount of liquid and circulates it naturally, so the residence time is long and thermal degradation proceeds more easily. The forced-circulation type flows the liquid through the tubes at high velocity to suppress boiling and prevent scale deposition, so it suits liquids that precipitate crystals and viscous liquids, but it needs pump power and is not aimed at a short residence time.

evaporation-015.question: Which statement correctly describes how the number of effects of a multiple-effect evaporator is chosen?
choices: Adding effects makes each body smaller and so lowers both the steam cost and the equipment cost, so the more effects the better for as long as the overall temperature difference allows

Adding effects cuts steam cost, but heat transfer area grows and boiling-point elevation eats into the overall temperature difference, so the number minimizing total steam and equipment cost is chosen
The number of effects is set by the condenser vacuum alone, unrelated to the boiling-point elevation, so effects can be added without limit by raising the vacuum
evaporation-015.explanation: Increasing the number of effects N cuts the live steam to roughly 1/N, but the effective temperature difference of each effect becomes smaller, so the total heat transfer area grows roughly in proportion to N. In addition, the boiling-point elevation is subtracted from the overall temperature difference in every effect, so for a solution with a large elevation the usable temperature difference shrinks as effects are added and soon reaches its limit. The number of effects is therefore chosen to minimize the annual sum of steam cost and equipment cost (depreciation). Seawater desalination, with a small boiling-point elevation, uses many effects, while concentrated electrolyte solutions use few. The idea that equipment cost also falls overlooks the increase in area. The condenser vacuum sets the lower end of the overall temperature difference, but the number of effects is decided by weighing boiling-point elevation and costs.
